source: Pauker and Kassirer (1975) Therapeutic decision making: a cost-benefit analysis
finding: First form of the therapeutic threshold. Treat if the chance of disease is above a threshold set by the benefit and harm of treatment. Withhold if below.
numbers: Single threshold. No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only (NEJM 293:229). Full equations not read. Assumes the chance of disease is known and utilities are fixed.
agent_relevance: A code rule can turn a probability plus benefit and harm numbers into act or do not act. This is the base of G5 style code decisions.

source: Pauker and Kassirer (1980) The threshold approach to clinical decision making
finding: Decision analysis gives two probability thresholds: a testing threshold and a test-treatment threshold. Below the first: do nothing. Above the second: treat without testing. Between them: test, then act on the result.
numbers: Two thresholds. Values come from test reliability (sensitivity, specificity), test risk, and treatment benefit and risk. NEJM 302(20):1109-1117, 15 May 1980.
quote: Treatment should be withheld if the probability of disease is smaller than the testing threshold
limits: Abstract only read (PubMed record). Worked cases and full equations not read. Needs a pretest probability the clinician can estimate; later work shows clinicians estimate it badly (see a12).
agent_relevance: S7 should only call a discriminating test when current belief sits between the two thresholds. Outside it, answer or stop. Thresholds can be computed in code.

source: Sox et al. (1986) Probability theory in the use of diagnostic tests: an introduction to critical study of the literature
finding: Teaches Bayes' theorem as the tool for test use. Pretest probability goes in, the test result updates it. Warns about pitfalls in estimating probability and about limits of studies of sensitivity and specificity.
numbers: No numbers in abstract (Ann Intern Med 104(1)).
limits: Abstract only read. Detail of the study limits (spectrum bias and similar) not read.
agent_relevance: Likelihood ratios taken from published accuracy studies may be inflated. An agent using them should keep ranges, not point values.

source: Sox et al. (1989) Threshold analysis using diagnostic tests with multiple results. Med Decis Making
finding: Extends the Pauker-Kassirer threshold model to a test that informs two relevant events at once (CT for mediastinal and hilar spread in lung cancer). Four thresholds appear.
numbers: Four thresholds. The range of prior probabilities where testing is best gets wider. Ignoring part of the test information leads to wrong test and treatment advice.
limits: Abstract only. Author list beyond Sox not confirmed in this session. One example (lung cancer staging).
agent_relevance: Tests with several outputs need all outputs used. A one-bit pass or fail S7 test may leave value on the table.

source: Casscells, Schoenberger and Graboys (1978) Interpretation by physicians of clinical laboratory results; replicated by Manrai et al. (2014) JAMA Intern Med
finding: Physicians were asked: prevalence 1/1000, false positive rate 5%, what is the chance a positive person has the disease? Most got it wrong. The 2013 replication found the same.
numbers: 1978 (Harvard, 60 people: 20 students, 20 interns, 20 attendings): 11 of 60 correct (18%); answer 95% given by 27 of 60 (45%). 2013 replication (61 people: 24 attendings, 26 house officers, 10 students, 1 retired): 14 of 61 correct (23%), difference 5% (95% CI -11% to 21%); 95% given by 27 of 61 (44%); median answer 66%, 33 times too high. Correct answer 1.96% (assuming perfect sensitivity).
quote: In both studies the most common answer was 95%
limits: Convenience samples. Question omits sensitivity (assumed 100%). Some respondents knew the PPV formula but mishandled prevalence. No improvement in 35 years.
agent_relevance: Base-rate neglect in test interpretation is stable and large. An agent must not trust a mental posterior. Compute it in code (G5).

source: Hoffrage and Gigerenzer (1998) Using natural frequencies to improve diagnostic inferences. Acad Med 73:538
finding: Physicians were asked for the positive predictive value of four tests. Probability format: 10% correct. Natural frequency format (counts from a reference group, not normalised by base rate): 46%.
numbers: 48 physicians in Munich and Dusseldorf, 4 problems. 10% correct with probabilities versus 46% with natural frequencies. Hemoccult example (prevalence 0.3%, sensitivity 50%, false positive 3%, true answer about 5%): answers ranged 1% to 99%; with frequencies 16 of 24 correct, with probabilities 1 of 24 (as quoted in a10).
limits: Small sample. Format mixed within physicians. A 2016 Medical Decision Making brief report reportedly argued part of the benefit is a scoring artefact (seen only in a search snippet, not opened). Still 54% wrong with frequencies.
agent_relevance: When the prompt gives counts (out of 1000 patients) the Bayes step is easier for people. For an LLM the same reformat may help, but code should do the arithmetic.

source: Hoffrage, Lindsey, Hertwig and Gigerenzer (2000) Communicating statistical information. Science 290:2261
finding: Perspective that experts, including medical staff, find combining statistics hard. Natural frequencies cut the difficulty. Uses in medicine, law and teaching.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Secondary sources report 44% to 68% correct with frequencies in this line of work; not verified here.
agent_relevance: Supports reformatting evidence as counts in S2 when a numeric belief step is needed.

source: McDowell and Jacobs (2017) Meta-analysis of the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning. Psychol Bull
finding: 35 articles, 226 performance estimates, 20 years. Natural frequencies help, but short formats and visual aids help both formats. Method factors such as seeing both formats change the rates.
numbers: 35 articles, 226 estimates. Average performance 24% with natural frequencies versus 4% with probabilities (quoted in the abstract of a09). Strongest moderators: short menu format and visual aids.
limits: About three quarters of participants still fail with frequencies. Two theories compete: ecological rationality and nested sets. Results depend on scoring and format exposure.
agent_relevance: A format trick alone will not fix base-rate use. Show the full calculation steps or compute in code.

source: Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies: frequency phobia in spite of probability blindness (2018)
finding: Many people given natural frequencies translate them back into probabilities and then fail. A switch to a harder format, linked to the Einstellung effect.
numbers: Cites 24% with frequencies versus 4% with probabilities from the meta-analysis.
limits: Abstract only. Sample sizes and authors not read.
agent_relevance: Models too may re-derive via conditional probabilities. A prompt should forbid format conversion and give one worked counting route.

source: Natural frequencies improve Bayesian reasoning in simple and complex inference tasks (Hoffrage, Krauss, Martignon, Gigerenzer 2015, Front Psychol)
finding: Extends natural frequencies to tests with three outcome values, three diseases, and two or three cues. Teaching on simple tasks transfers to complex ones.
numbers: Study 1, medical students: frequencies raise Bayesian inferences by an average of 37 percentage points across four complex conditions. Study 2: after teaching, 40% correct (three cue values) and 81% (two cues). Introduction restates the hemoccult result: 16 of 24 physicians vs 1 of 24.
limits: Students, not working clinicians. Abstract and introduction read; method tables not read. Authors and title taken from memory, page title not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Frequency format is not limited to one binary test. It extends to several tests in sequence, useful for a multi-test S7.

source: Gill, Sabin and Schmid (2005) Why clinicians are natural Bayesians. BMJ
finding: Argues clinicians use Bayesian-like updating in practice without formal numbers.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Only a one-line abstract read. Sits against a12 and a05, where explicit probability estimates are poor.
agent_relevance: Informal likelihood sense may exist but explicit numbers fail. Keep verbal evidence strength and map it to numbers in code.

source: Morgan et al. (2021) Accuracy of practitioner estimates of probability of diagnosis before and after testing. JAMA Intern Med
finding: 553 practitioners overestimated pretest probability in all four scenarios and overestimated post-test probability, after both positive and negative results.
numbers: 553 complete answers (290 residents, 202 attendings, 61 NP/PA) of 723 asked. Positive result: pneumonia 95% (evidence 46-65%), breast cancer after mammogram 50% (3-9%), cardiac ischemia after stress test 70% (2-11%), UTI after culture 80% (0-8.3%). Negative result: pneumonia 50% (10-19%), breast 5% (<0.05%), ischemia 5% (0.43-2.5%), UTI 5% (0-0.11%). Implied positive LRs: pneumonia 4.8 (evidence 2.6), mammography 44.3 (13-33), stress test 21.0 (2.0-2.7), urine culture 9.0 (9.0). Negative LR mammography 1.0 (0.05-0.24), stress test 0.6 (0.5-0.6).
limits: Survey of written vignettes; reference values from an expert literature review, given as ranges. Adjustment varied by test: urine culture and chest film LRs matched the evidence.
agent_relevance: Current practice errs by overstating. An agent should hold a table of likelihood ratios with ranges and update in code, not recall them.

source: Rodman, Buckley, Manrai and Morgan (2023) AI vs clinician performance in estimating probabilities of diagnoses before and after testing. JAMA Netw Open
finding: GPT-4 was given the Morgan survey cases, 100 samples each at temperature 1.0 (21 Oct 2023). It had less error than clinicians after a negative result in all 5 cases. After a positive result it was better in 2 cases, similar in 2, worse in 1.
numbers: Median LLM vs clinician: pneumonia pretest 72 vs 80; breast cancer pretest 1 vs 5; after positive mammogram 8 vs 50 (reference 3-9); cardiac ischemia after positive stress test 69 vs 70 (reference 2-11, both wrong); asymptomatic bacteriuria pretest 26 vs 20 (MAE 26.2 vs 32.2). Hypothetical-testing case: LLM 2% after positive (MAE 0.04) vs humans 95% (MAE 74.4).
limits: Simple prompt, simplistic cases, one model. Narrow LLM spread partly explains lower error. Misread asymptomatic bacteriuria as UTI. Authors say the weaker positive-test results are not explained.
agent_relevance: GPT-4 estimates are less wild than human ones but still wrong on the stress-test positive LR. Use code with a likelihood-ratio table.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (o1-preview)
finding: o1-preview was strong on differential diagnosis and reasoning quality, but on the Morgan probabilistic cases it performed about like GPT-4.
numbers: 100 outputs per question. Table 3 medians o1-preview / GPT-4 / clinicians (n=553): pneumonia pretest 70 / 72 / 80; pneumonia after positive 94.9 / 95 / 95; breast cancer after positive 2.8 / 7.8 / 50 (ref 3-9); cardiac ischemia after positive 10.9 / 68.7 / 70 (ref 2-11); UTI after positive 90 / 90 / 80 (ref 0-8.3); UTI pretest 15 / 25.6 / 20 (ref 0-1). MAE cardiac ischemia after positive: 5.7 vs 56.5 (GPT-4) vs 56.3 (clinicians).
quote: o1-preview performs similarly to GPT-4 in estimating pre-test and post-test probabilities
limits: o1-preview and GPT-4 similar except stress test, where o1 moved much closer to reference. Pneumonia pretest and UTI estimates stay far from reference. Table shows four cases; text says five.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model fixes one case, not all. Probability estimates still rest on recalled knowledge; supply them from a retrieved table.

source: Li and Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of large language models
finding: LLMs show two modes. When all numbers are given they follow Bayes' rule. When base rate or diagnosticity must be recalled, they judge by similarity (representativeness) and ignore base rates.
numbers: Structured test: 15 models, top models beat humans. Jason test (75 vs 25 base rate; normative posterior-odds ratio 9): uncharacteristic description gave posteriors 0.75 vs 0.25 for GPT-4o, GPT-4, Claude-3-Opus (ratio 9, 9, 8.86); humans 0.63 vs 0.43 (ratio 2.25). For representative descriptions all LLMs had a ratio near 1. Prior vs posterior Spearman about -0.84 to -0.90; posterior vs similarity 0.87 to 0.94. GPT-4o gave priors of 2-4% when asked alone but used 10-30% when judging.
limits: Preprint. Six models in the semi-structured test. Personality-vignette task, not clinical. Changing one prompt word (compute posterior) could flip behaviour to Bayes, but stronger prompts did not always work in the unstructured test.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5: ask for components (prior, likelihoods) separately and compute the posterior in code. A model's recalled prior is unstable.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (SDBench, MAI-DxO)
finding: 304 NEJM case benchmark with costs. A panel scaffold with a hypothesis role updating probabilities in a Bayesian way and a test-chooser role picking maximally discriminating tests beat off-the-shelf models on cost and accuracy.
numbers: Physicians 20% accuracy at $2,963; GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745; o3 78.6% at $7,850; MAI-DxO with o3 79.9% at $2,397, 81.9% at $4,735, and 85.5% at $7,184 (ensemble).
limits: Probabilities are written by the model, no calibration shown. Many scaffold parts changed at once (debate, cost tracker, checklist), so the effect of test choice alone is not isolated. Gatekeeper is an LLM. Chain of debate conflicts with our G9 no-debate rule.
agent_relevance: S7 style test choice (discriminating tests plus stewardship) is supported. Cost control alone cut spend 70% vs o3 with similar accuracy.

source: Ruhrberg Estevez, Astorga and van der Schaar (2025) ACTMED: timely clinical diagnosis through active test selection. NeurIPS
finding: Picks the next test by expected KL divergence from prior to simulated posterior, using the LLM to simulate outcomes. Stops when the expected gain is small.
numbers: Tasks: CKD, hepatitis C, diabetes, OSCE. Budget of 3 tests, 5 seeds, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o. Beat implicit LLM selection on hepatitis and diabetes, even above the full-information baseline. KL-based stopping cut tests by nearly 50% with comparable or better accuracy. Implicit LLM selection mostly chose globally best features and did not personalise.
limits: Tabular datasets, not open clinical cases. Exact accuracy values only in figures, not extracted. LLM-simulated outcome distributions only partly checked.
agent_relevance: Expected information gain plus a stop rule is a code-implementable S7 and S4 stop rule.

source: Jia, Pu, Guo and Agrawal (2025) Counting clues: a lightweight probabilistic baseline can match an LLM
finding: A smoothed Naive Bayes over concept-diagnosis co-occurrence counts from pretraining corpora matches LLMs on MedQA diagnosis questions, and the two are right on different questions.
numbers: MedQA diagnosis subset n=719, five options: FBPR on Dolma 46.7% vs OLMo Instruct 44.1%, hybrid 47.3%. RedPajama FBPR 44.5% vs LLaMA 65B 47.0%, hybrid 50.8%. MedMCQA diagnosis n=639 (4 options): FBPR 52.7%. Both correct 24.8% vs 20.6% expected under independence. Where the methods agree (38.3% of questions), 64.7% are correct.
limits: Counts depend on a concept extractor. Multiple choice, not sequential. Matching accuracy shows co-occurrence explains much, not that LLMs use it.
agent_relevance: A frequency prior is a cheap second signal. Agreement between two unlike methods marks reliable answers (supports code-side agreement checks).

source: Qiu et al. (2025, v3 2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs fall far short of a Bayesian Assistant at updating beliefs about a user's preferences over 5 rounds. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian model's guesses raises agreement to about 80% and generalises to other tasks.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds, 100 new option sets per round; Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro; human subset 48 users. LLMs showed little gain after round 1. Bayesian-tuned models agreed with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time, more than oracle-tuned.
limits: Fine-tuning, outside our no-training setting. Task is preference learning, not medical tests.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone leaves belief updating weak. Supports doing updates in code.

source: Djulbegovic et al. (2015) Rationality, practice variation and person-centred health policy: a threshold hypothesis
finding: Practice differences are explained by different probability thresholds for acting. Regret and context shift thresholds. Current regulation pushes thresholds low, favouring overuse of tests and treatment.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Argues for a testable threshold model based on reflective equilibrium; no data in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Thresholds are not fixed facts. They depend on the cost of error. Set them per task from an explicit cost of a wrong answer.

source: Djulbegovic et al. (2015) Dual processing model for medical decision-making: an extension to diagnostic testing
finding: Compares an expected-utility test threshold with a dual-processing one that adds intuitive (type 1) views of benefit and harm. The second explains testing decisions better in a prostate cancer case.
numbers: No numbers in abstract. One case vignette.
limits: Abstract only. No data fit in the abstract. If type 1 dominates, ordering a test does not change the decision.
agent_relevance: Check that a test result can actually change the action. A test run after the answer is fixed adds nothing.

source: Eddy (1982) Probabilistic reasoning in clinical medicine: problems and opportunities (in Kahneman, Slovic, Tversky eds., Judgment under Uncertainty)
finding: Physicians confuse the chance of a positive given disease with the chance of disease given a positive. Classic mammography problem.
numbers: From memory, not opened here: prevalence 1%, sensitivity about 79%, false positive about 9.6%, true posterior about 7.5%; most of 100 physicians estimated about 75%.
limits: Not read this session. Numbers must be verified before use.
agent_relevance: Origin of the confusion of the inverse. Same error as a05 and a12.

source: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats. Psychol Rev 102
finding: Introduced the natural frequency account: the mind handles counts from natural sampling better than normalised probabilities.
numbers: From memory, not opened: Bayesian answers rose from about 16% (probabilities) to about 46% (frequencies) over 15 problems. Verify. The 24% vs 4% in a08 is from a later meta-analysis.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Founding paper of the frequency-format approach used in a06 to a10.

source: Fagan (1975) Letter: nomogram for Bayes's theorem. NEJM 293:257
finding: A one-page chart to go from pretest probability and a likelihood ratio to post-test probability, with no calculator.
numbers: No abstract found. From memory: three scales, pretest probability, likelihood ratio, post-test probability.
limits: Only the PubMed record was found; no text read.
agent_relevance: The odds form (posterior odds = prior odds x LR) is what G5 code should run, chaining LRs only for conditionally independent tests.

source: Kassirer (1989) Our stubborn quest for diagnostic certainty: a cause of excessive testing. NEJM 320:1489
finding: Argues that chasing certainty drives low-yield tests. A test only helps if its result could change the action.
numbers: No abstract found. Content from memory.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Supports stop rules in S7: no test when the posterior stays on one side of the treatment threshold.
